questions.text: An unresponsive patient regains a pulse after defibrillation for ventricular fibrillation, and the post-shock ECG shows third-degree AV block with a slow ventricular rate. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.explanation: With a pulse present, symptomatic complete heart block is treated with transcutaneous pacing (± dopamine/epinephrine infusion) rather than defibrillation or chest compressions, which are reserved for pulseless rhythms.
questions.note: Without a pulse, this is PEA: resume CPR and give epinephrine; routine pacing during established arrest is not recommended.

questions.text: The recovered ECG shows P waves marching out independently from QRS complexes at a faster rate than the ventricular rate, with no fixed relationship between P and QRS. What is the diagnosis? [img: ERArrhythmia1.png ]
options: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block
originalOptions: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block
questions.explanation: Complete AV dissociation — P waves and QRS complexes occurring independently with the atrial rate faster than the ventricular escape rate — defines third-degree AV block, unlike Mobitz I/II where some P waves still conduct.

questions.text: Which statement correctly differentiates Mobitz type I from Mobitz type II second-degree AV block?

Both types show progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat
Mobitz II is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS and low risk of complete block

Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation until a P wave is not conducted and is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS; Mobitz II has constant PR intervals with sudden nonconducted beats and is usually infranodal with a wide QRS

questions.text: A 12-lead ECG shows a constant PR interval of 240 ms with every P wave followed by a QRS complex. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A fixed PR interval >200 ms with 1:1 conduction (no dropped beats) defines first-degree AV block, a partial delay rather than an interruption of conduction.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia2.png ] The ECG shows constant PR intervals with intermittent nonconducted P waves in a patient with an acute anterior wall MI. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give atropine only, with no further action
Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
originalOptions: Give atropine only, with no further action
Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
questions.correctAnswer: E) Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
questions.correctAnswerText: Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
questions.explanation: Mobitz II or high-grade AV block complicating anterior MI reflects extensive infranodal conduction system damage and can progress abruptly to complete block/asystole, so urgent pacing readiness and cardiology evaluation are required rather than observation or AV-nodal blocking drugs.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia3.png ] An asymptomatic 29-year-old has first-degree AV block on this ECG with no other conduction disease. What is the best next step?
options: No acute treatment; review medications and confirm the cause

questions.explanation: Isolated, asymptomatic first-degree AV block requires no acute intervention beyond identifying reversible causes (e.g., AV-nodal blocking drugs); cardioversion and defibrillation are irrelevant since this is not a tachyarrhythma

questions.text: What are the defining ECG features of complete (third-degree) AV block?
options: Progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
Fixed PR interval with intermittent nonconducted P waves
Constant PR interval >200 ms with 1:1 conduction
originalOptions: Progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
Fixed PR interval with intermittent nonconducted P waves
Constant PR interval >200 ms with 1:1 conduction
questions.correctAnswer: B) Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
questions.correctAnswerText: Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
questions.explanation: In third-degree block, P waves and QRS complexes occur completely independently (AV dissociation), with the atrial rate faster than the escape ventricular rate; the escape QRS is narrow if junctional, wide if ventricular/infranodal.

questions.text: What ECG finding is diagnostic of complete (third-degree) heart block?
options: Fixed PR interval with dropped beats
Short PR interval with a delta wave
Irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes
originalOptions: Fixed PR interval with dropped beats
Short PR interval with a delta wave
Irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes
questions.correctAnswer: E) Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes
questions.correctAnswerText: Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes
questions.explanation: The hallmark of complete heart block is total dissociation of atrial and ventricular activity — P waves and QRS complexes occur independently at their own rates.

questions.text: A patient develops Mobitz II AV block complicating an acute anterior wall MI. When is a permanent pacemaker indicated?
options: Only if the patient develops asystole
Never; anterior MI-related block always resolves
If the infranodal block persists despite treatment of reversible causes, since anterior MI-related block reflects extensive septal damage and carries a high risk of progression

questions.correctAnswerText: If the infranodal block persists despite treatment of reversible causes, since anterior MI-related block reflects extensive septal damage and carries a high risk of progression
questions.explanation: Anterior MI causing Mobitz II/high-grade block indicates extensive septal/infranodal damage with a high risk of sudden complete block or asystole; if it persists after reversible causes are addressed, permanent pacing is indicated.

questions.text: A patient has atrial fibrillation of unknown duration and is hemodynamically stable. What anticoagulation strategy should precede elective cardioversion?
options: Therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks before and 4 weeks after cardioversion, or a TEE-guided strategy with peri- and post-procedural anticoagulation
No anticoagulation needed if cardioversion restores sinus rhythm
Anticoagulation is only needed after cardioversion, not before

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia4.png] A hemodynamically stable patient has atrial flutter with a ventricular rate around 130/min and no heart-failure symptoms. What is the best initial treatment?
options: A beta-blocker for ventricular rate control
originalOptions: A beta-blocker for ventricular rate control

questions.explanation: In stable atrial flutter, rate control with a beta-blocker (or diltiazem/verapamil if LVEF is preserved) is first-line; cardioversion is reserved for instability, and adenosine only transiently unmasks flutter waves without terminating the rhythm.

questions.text: Which arrhythmia is most commonly associated with thyrotoxicosis?
questions.explanation: Thyrotoxicosis sensitizes atrial myocardium and is a classic reversible cause of atrial fibrillation; thyroid function should be checked in all new-onset AF.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia5.png] What rhythm is shown on this 12-lead ECG?
questions.explanation: The tracing shows an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm without discrete P waves, replaced by fine fibrillatory baseline oscillations — diagnostic of atrial fibrillation.

questions.text: A patient has symptomatic bradycardia with a heart rate of 32/min and a palpable pulse. Which of the following are acceptable therapeutic options if the initial drug is ineffective?
options: Atropine, followed by transcutaneous pacing and/or dopamine or epinephrine infusion
Immediate chest compressions regardless of pulse
Observation only, since bradycardia is never treated pharmacologically
originalOptions: Atropine, followed by transcutaneous pacing and/or dopamine or epinephrine infusion
Immediate chest compressions regardless of pulse
Observation only, since bradycardia is never treated pharmacologically
questions.correctAnswer: A) Atropine, followed by transcutaneous pacing and/or dopamine or epinephrine infusion
questions.correctAnswerText: Atropine, followed by transcutaneous pacing and/or dopamine or epinephrine infusion
questions.explanation: Atropine is first-line for symptomatic bradycardia with a pulse; if ineffective, transcutaneous pacing and/or a chronotropic infusion are next-line options per the adult bradycardia algorithm.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia5.png] An adult patient has symptomatic bradycardia with a pulse and poor perfusion. What is the correct approach to management?
options: Chest compressions, invasive airway, transcutaneous pacing
Support ABCs and give atropine; if ineffective, use transcutaneous pacing and/or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion

questions.explanation: Since the patient has a pulse, chest compressions and defibrillation are not indicated; the adult bradycardia algorithm proceeds from atropine to pacing/chronotropic infusion if there is inadequate response.

questions.text: What is the first-line medication to treat symptomatic bradycardia?
questions.explanation: Atropine is the first drug given in the adult symptomatic bradycardia algorithm because it reverses excessive vagal tone at the SA/AV node; beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers would worsen bradycardia.

questions.text: A patient has symptomatic bradycardia with cardiopulmonary compromise. What is the correct atropine dosing and next step if ineffective?
options: Atropine 5 mg IV bolus, single dose
Atropine 1 mg IV every 3-5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg

questions.correctAnswerText: Atropine 1 mg IV every 3-5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg
questions.explanation: Current ACLS bradycardia dosing is atropine 1 mg IV push every 3-5 minutes (max 3 mg); persistent symptomatic bradycardia despite atropine warrants pacing or a chronotropic infusion while reversible causes are treated.

questions.text: Which of the following is an EXTRINSIC (reversible) cause of bradycardia rather than intrinsic SA-node disease?
options: Increased vagal tone or drug effect
originalOptions: Increased vagal tone or drug effect
questions.correctAnswer: A) Increased vagal tone or drug effect
questions.correctAnswerText: Increased vagal tone or drug effect
questions.explanation: Extrinsic bradycardia results from reversible factors like vagal stimulation, drugs, hypothyroidism, or raised ICP, distinguishing it from intrinsic structural SA-node disease such as sick sinus syndrome or fibrosis.

questions.text: Which of the following is a pathological, intrinsic cause of bradycardia rather than a normal physiological variant?
options: High resting vagal tone in a trained athlete
Respiratory sinus arrhythmia in a healthy child
originalOptions: High resting vagal tone in a trained athlete
Respiratory sinus arrhythmia in a healthy child
questions.explanation: Sick sinus syndrome reflects intrinsic structural SA-node disease (typically idiopathic fibrosis), unlike athletic bradycardia, sleep-related bradycardia, or respiratory sinus arrhythmia, which are normal physiological findings.

questions.text: What is the first clinical issue assessed in the bradycardia algorithm?

Whether the bradycardia is causing cardiopulmonary compromise/poor perfusion

questions.explanation: The bradycardia algorithm begins by determining whether the slow rate is causing symptomatic hypoperfusion, since this determines whether pharmacologic/electrical treatment is needed or the patient can be observed.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia6.png] A 55-year-old asthmatic patient presents with palpitations. and she is hemodynamically stable. What is the best next step for management?
questions.explanation: In stable AF, rate control is first-line; diltiazem is preferred over a beta-blocker in this asthmatic patient to avoid bronchospasm, while adenosine and atropine have no role in AF.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia19.png] A 73-year-old ICU patient becomes unresponsive with a tachyarrhythmia on ECG and a blood pressure of 70/40. What is the best next step for management?
questions.explanation: A tachyarrhythmia causing severe hypotension and unresponsiveness is unstable; immediate synchronized cardioversion is indicated rather than pharmacologic rate/rhythm control

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia7.png] A patient becomes unresponsive and the ECG shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the immediate next step?
options: Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation with high-quality CPR

questions.text: How is adult asystolic cardiac arrest managed?
options: Confirm true asystole in at least two leads, begin/continue high-quality CPR, give epinephrine as soon as possible and every 3-5 minutes, and treat reversible causes
Transcutaneous pacing as the first intervention

questions.explanation: Asystole is not a shockable rhythm; management relies on high-quality CPR and epinephrine, with a search for reversible causes (Hs and Ts), rather than defibrillation or routine pacing.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia8.png] A young athlete collapses and the his ECG. What is the rhythm?
questions.explanation: The twisting QRS axis around the isoelectric baseline is characteristic of torsades de pointes, a polymorphic VT associated with QT prolongation (e.g., congenital long-QT syndrome in a young patient).

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia9.png] An 85-year-old previously healthy woman presents with recurrent syncope, the last episode an hour ago. Her ECG shows a fixed PR interval with intermittently nonconducted P waves. What type of block does she have?
questions.explanation: A constant PR interval with sudden, unpredicted dropped QRS complexes (no progressive lengthening) defines Mobitz type II, an infranodal block with a high risk of progression to complete heart block — consistent with her syncope.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia8.png] An ICU patient becomes unresponsive with no pulse and is not breathing. What is the best next step?
questions.explanation: Pulseless polymorphic VT (torsades) is treated as a shockable rhythm; immediate defibrillation takes priority over airway management or drug administration.

questions.text: Which intervention provides the greatest immediate survival benefit in ventricular fibrillation?
options: Early unsynchronized defibrillation combined with high-quality CPR
originalOptions: Early unsynchronized defibrillation combined with high-quality CPR
questions.correctAnswer: E) Early unsynchronized defibrillation combined with high-quality CPR
questions.correctAnswerText: Early unsynchronized defibrillation combined with high-quality CPR
questions.explanation: Time to defibrillation is the strongest predictor of survival in VF; CPR maintains perfusion until a shock can be delivered, while drugs and airway management are adjunctive.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia10.png] This ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves, a broad notched R wave in V5/V6, and deep S waves in V1/V2. What two abnormalities are present?

questions.text: What is the most important immediate precursor/risk factor for pulmonary embolism?

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia11.png] An athletic patient presents with a racing heart sensation and stable vitals. The ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia. What do you give?
questions.explanation: For a stable, regular narrow-complex (likely SVT) tachycardia, vagal maneuvers followed by IV adenosine is first-line; diltiazem/verapamil are second-line alternatives, and atropine/amiodarone have no role here.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia12.png] A patient has normal vital signs with a heart rate of 170/min. The ECG shows a regular, monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia. What do you give?
questions.explanation: In stable, regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia (presumed VT with a pulse), an antiarrhythmic infusion such as amiodarone is appropriate with expert consultation; diltiazem/verapamil should be avoided in wide-complex tachycardia of uncertain origin.

questions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia13.png] Progressive PR-interval prolongation followed by a dropped QRS complex identifies which rhythm?
questions.correctAnswer: D) Second-degree AV block, Mobitz I (Wenckebach)
questions.explanation: Progressive PR lengthening culminating in a nonconducted P wave, with the cycle then repeating, is the defining feature of Mobitz I (Wenckebach) block.

allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Capitate
allQuestions.explanation: The capitate is the largest carpal bone, centrally located in the distal carpal row, distinguishing it from the hamate (ulnar side), lunate (proximal row), and trapezoid (radial side).
